NARM combines the final GRU state with an attention-weighted sum of hidden states through concatenation and bilinear scoring; its fusion is not an explicit sigmoid gate. On DIGINETICA, d=100, hybrid Recall@20 is 62.58 versus 61.88 global-only and 61.71 attention-only: evidence for complementary representations, not learned gating specifically. [NARM](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1711.04725). STAMP is closely related session-interest prior art, but its original paper was inaccessible here; no verified numerical gating ablation obtained. [Author implementation](https://github.com/uestcnlp/STAMP).

SLi-Rec supplies the clearest direct gating control: α=σ(W[short,long,context]+b), followed by α·short+(1−α)·long. Context includes time interval and target-item embedding, so this is candidate-dependent fusion rather than a reusable SASRec residual. Adaptive versus fixed-fusion AUC: Electronics .8282/.8274, Movies .8769/.8725, CDs .9279/.9261. Gains exist but vary substantially; these classification results do not establish sampled HR@10 gains. [SLi-Rec, Table 5](https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/research/uploads/prod/2019/07/IJCAI19-ready_v1.pdf).

SASRec already preserves recent-item information through residual connections. Removing residuals reduces Beauty NDCG@10 from .3142 to .2591; zero attention blocks, effectively last-item-only, reaches .2620. Thus an added recent-item branch may duplicate existing capacity. [SASRec, Table IV](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1808.09781). Suggested inexpensive controls, inferred from these findings: unchanged SASRec; last-item residual; masked recent-k mean and exponential-recency pooling; tuned constant residual weight; learned global scalar; history-conditioned scalar/vector gate; attention pooling with identical fusion. Hold objective, sampling, embeddings and training budget constant. The reviewed ablations do not establish that adaptive gating beats fixed recency pooling; test that distinction before prioritizing it over objective changes.
